nameStory: The 'crowded parchment' gets its name from its papery, thin texture that feels remarkably like old parchment paper when you touch it. The 'crowded' part comes from how these fungi cluster together in overlapping tiers on dead wood, creating dense, shelf-like formations that can cover entire sections of fallen logs.
description: Crowded parchment is a bracket fungus that forms thin, leathery shelves on dead hardwood trees and logs. These overlapping, fan-shaped brackets have a smooth, tan to grayish upper surface and typically measure 1-3 inches across. Unlike mushrooms with caps and stems, this species grows directly from the wood surface in tiered clusters that can extend for several feet along a log.

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Forms overlapping, tiered brackets that grow in dense clusters along dead logs, creating a shingle-like appearance

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels thin and papery like parchment when dry, becoming slightly flexible when fresh and moist

idTips.label: Upper Surface
idTips.description: Smooth and often zoned with concentric rings, ranging from tan to grayish-brown, sometimes with a slight sheen

idTips.label: Lower Surface
idTips.description: Smooth and cream to pale orange, lacking the pores or gills found in other bracket fungi

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual brackets typically 1-3 inches wide and quite thin, usually less than 1/4 inch thick

habitat: Look for crowded parchment on dead branches and logs of hardwood trees throughout New England's forests, from sea level to mountain elevations. It's particularly common on oak, maple, and beech, favoring fallen logs and dead standing wood in both mature forests and woodland edges.

seasonality.spring: Fresh brackets begin developing after spring rains, appearing as small, light-colored growths that are soft and pliable to the touch.
seasonality.summer: Active growth continues with brackets expanding and developing their characteristic concentric zones and smooth surfaces.
seasonality.fall: Brackets reach maturity and begin hardening, becoming more papery and brittle as moisture levels drop.
seasonality.winter: Persistent year-round, old brackets become very dry and brittle but remain visible on logs, often lasting through multiple seasons.

funFact: Despite being called 'parchment,' this fungus is actually helping to recycle the forest by breaking down lignin, one of the toughest components of wood - essentially performing the same job as a tiny lumber mill, turning solid logs back into soil nutrients!
confusionNotes: Often confused with turkey tail, but crowded parchment has a smooth underside while turkey tail has tiny pores. Remember: if you can't see pores underneath, you're likely looking at a parchment fungus, not turkey tail.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Stereum comes from Greek meaning 'solid' or 'firm,' which might seem odd for such a thin fungus, but refers to the tough, leathery texture that allows these brackets to persist for years on dead wood.
compareHints: Among its Stereum relatives, crowded parchment is distinguished by its particularly thin, papery texture and tendency to form the most densely overlapping clusters. Unlike the hairy curtain crust which has a fuzzy upper surface, or the bleeding crusts which ooze red liquid when cut, crowded parchment maintains its smooth, dry parchment-like appearance and doesn't bleed when damaged.

relatedSpecies.distinction: False turkeytail differs from other Stereum species by its distinctive concentric color bands that closely mimic true turkey tail.
